entries.38ba70e09b1dc90f277c8e4a85a32b7402ab72f6: <div sID="gen17470" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Jer.13" sID="Jer.13"/> <div eID="gen17470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17471" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17472" type="x-p"/> Still the prophet is attempting to awaken this secure and stubborn people to repentance, by the consideration of the judgments of God that were coming upon them. He is to tell them, I. By the sign of a girdle spoiled that their pride should be stained, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. By the sign of bottles filled with wine that their counsels should be blasted, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.12-Jer.13.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. III. In consideration hereof he is to call them to repent and humble themselves, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.15-Jer.13.21">ver. 15-21</reference>. IV. He is to convince them that it is for their obstinacy and incorrigibleness that the judgments of God are so prolonged and brought to extremity, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.22-Jer.13.27">ver. 22-27</reference>.
entries.7e719db7233dfa1e5afda6664e9ecfbafc7d3f92: <div eID="gen17472" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17471" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Marred Girdle. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17473" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto me, Go and get thee a linen girdle, and put it upon thy loins, and put it not in water. <hi type="super">2</hi> So I got a girdle according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on my loins. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me the second time, saying, <hi type="super">4</hi> Take the girdle that thou hast got, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon thy loins, and arise, go to Euphrates, and hide it there in a hole of the rock. <hi type="super">5</hi> So I went, and hid it by Euphrates, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded me. <hi type="super">6</hi> And it came to pass after many days, that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, Arise, go to Euphrates, and take the girdle from thence, which I commanded thee to hide there. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then I went to Euphrates, and digged, and took the girdle from the place where I had hid it: and, behold, the girdle was marred, it was profitable for nothing. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">9</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , After this manner will I mar the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">10</hi> This evil people, which refuse to hear my words, which walk in the imagination of their heart, and walk after other gods, to serve them, and to worship them, shall even be as this girdle, which is good for nothing. <hi type="super">11</hi> For as the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, so have I caused to cleave unto me the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; that they might be unto me for a people, and for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory: but they would not hear. <div eID="gen17473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17474" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A sign, the marring of a girdle, which the prophet had worn for some time, by hiding it in a hole of a rock near the river Euphrates. It was usual with the prophets to teach by signs, that a stupid unthinking people might be brought to consider, and believe, and be affected with what was thus set before them. 1. He was to wear a linen girdle for some time, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Some think he wore it under his clothes, because it was linen, and it is said to <hi type="italic">cleave to his loins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">v. 11</reference>. It should rather seem to be worn upon his clothes, for it was worn for a name and a praise, and probably was a fine sash, such as officers wear and such as are commonly worn at this day in the eastern nations. He must <hi type="italic">not put it in water,</hi> but wear it as it was, that it might be the stronger, and less likely to rot: linen wastes almost as much with washing as with wearing. Being not wet, it was the more stiff and less apt to bend, yet he must make a shift to wear it. Probably it was very fine linen which will wear long without washing. The prophet, like John Baptist, was none of those that wore soft clothing, and therefore it would be the more strange to see him with a linen girdle on, who probably used to wear a leathern one. 2. After he had worn this linen girdle for some time, he must go, and <hi type="italic">hide it in a hole of a rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.4">v. 4</reference>) by the water's side, where, when the water was high, it would be wet, and when it fell would grow dry again, and by that means would soon rot, sooner than if it were always wet or always dry. 3. After many days, he must look for it, and he should find it quite spoiled, gone all to rags and good for nothing, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.7">v. 7</reference>. It has been of old a question among interpreters whether this was really done, so as to be seen and observed by the people, or only in a dream or vision, so as to go no further than the prophet's own mind. It seems hard to imagine that the prophet should be sent on two such long journeys as to the river Euphrates, each of which would take him up some week's time, when he could so ill be spared at home. For this reason most incline to think the journey, at least, was only in vision, like that of Ezekiel, from the captivity in Chaldea to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.3">Ezek. viii. 3</reference>) and thence back to Chaldea (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.24">ch. xi. 24</reference>); and the explanation of this sign is given only to the prophet himself (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.8">v. 8</reference>), not to the people, the sign not being public. But there being, it is probable, at that time, great conveniences of travelling between Jerusalem and Babylon, and some part of Euphrates being not so far off but that it was made the utmost border of the land of promise (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.4">Josh. i. 4</reference>), I see no inconvenience in supposing the prophet to have made two journeys thither; for it is expressly said, <hi type="italic">He did as the Lord commanded him;</hi> and thus gave a signal proof of his obsequiousness to his God, to shame the stubbornness of a disobedient people: the toil of his journey would be very proper to signify both the pains they took to corrupt themselves with their idolatries and the sad fatigue of their captivity; and Euphrates being the river of Babylon, which was to be the place of their bondage, was a material circumstance in this sign. <div eID="gen17474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17475" type="x-p"/> II. The thing signified by this sign. The prophet was willing to be at any cost and pains to affect this people with the word of the Lord. Ministers must spend, and be spent, for the good of souls. We have the explanation of this sign, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.9-Jer.13.11">v. 9-11</reference>. <div eID="gen17475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17476" type="x-p"/> 1. The people of Israel had been to God as this girdle in two respects:—(1.) He had taken them into covenant and communion with himself: <hi type="italic">As the girdle cleaves</hi> very closely <hi type="italic">to the loins of a man</hi> and surrounds him, <hi type="italic">so have I caused to cleave to me the houses of Israel and Judah.</hi> They were a people near to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.148.14">Ps. cxlviii. 14</reference>); they were his own, a peculiar people to him, a kingdom of priests that had access to him above other nations. He <hi type="italic">caused them to cleave</hi> to him by the law he gave them, the prophets he sent among them, and the favours which in his providence he showed them. He required their stated attendance in the courts of his house, and the frequent ratification of their covenant with him by sacrifices. Thus they were made so as to cleave to him that one would think they could never have been parted. (2.) He had herein designed his own honour. When he took them to be <hi type="italic">to him for a people,</hi> it was that they might be to him <hi type="italic">for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory,</hi> as a girdle is an ornament to a man, and particularly the <hi type="italic">curious girdle of the ephod</hi> was to the high-priest <hi type="italic">for glory and for beauty.</hi> Note, Those whom God takes to be to him for a people he intends to be to him for a praise. [1.] It is their duty to honour him, by observing his institutions and aiming therein at his glory, and thus adorning their profession. [2.] It is their happiness that he reckons himself honoured in them and by them. He is pleased with them, and glories in his relation to them, while they behave themselves as become his people. He was pleased to take it among the titles of his honour to be <hi type="italic">the God of Israel,</hi> even a <hi type="italic">God to Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.24">1 Chron. xvii. 24</reference>. In vain do we pretend to be to God for a people if we be not to him for a praise. <div eID="gen17476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17477" type="x-p"/> 2. They had by their idolatries and other iniquities loosed themselves from him, thrown themselves at a distance, robbed him of the honour they owed him, buried themselves in the earth, and foreign earth too, mingled among the nations, and were so spoiled and corrupted that they were <hi type="italic">good for nothing:</hi> they could no more be to God, as they were designed, <hi type="italic">for a name and a praise,</hi> for they would not hear either their duty to do it or their privilege to value it: <hi type="italic">They refused to hear the words of God,</hi> by which they might have been kept still cleaving closely to him. <hi type="italic">They walked in the imagination of their heart,</hi> wherever their fancy led them; and denied themselves no gratification they had a mind to, particularly in their worship. They would not <hi type="italic">cleave to God,</hi> but <hi type="italic">walked after other gods, to serve them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to worship them;</hi> they doted upon the gods of the heathen nations that lay towards Euphrates, so that they were quite spoiled for the service of their own God, and were as <hi type="italic">this girdle,</hi> this rotten girdle, a disgrace to their profession and not an ornament. A thousand pities it was that such a girdle should be so spoiled, that such a people should so wretchedly degenerate. <div eID="gen17477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17478" type="x-p"/> 3. God would by his judgments separate them from him, send them into captivity, deface all their beauty and ruin their excellency, so that they should be like a fine girdle gone to rags, a worthless, useless, despicable people. God will after this manner <hi type="italic">mar the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem.</hi> He would strip them of all that which was the matter of their pride, of which they boasted and in which they trusted; it should not only be sullied and stained, but quite destroyed, like this linen girdle. Observe, He speaks of <hi type="italic">the pride of Judah</hi> (the country people were proud of their holy land, their good land), but of <hi type="italic">the great pride of Jerusalem;</hi> there the temple was, and the royal palace, and therefore those citizens were more proud than the inhabitants of other cities. God takes notice of the degrees of men's pride, the pride of some and the great pride of others; and he will mar it, he will stain it. Pride will have a fall, for God resists the proud. He will either mar the pride that is in us (that is, mortify it by his grace, make us ashamed of it, and, like Hezekiah, humble us for the pride of our hearts, the great pride, and cure us of it, great as it is; and this marring of the pride will be making of the soul; happy for us if the humbling providences our hearts be humbled) or else he will mar the thing we are proud of. Parts, gifts, learning, power, external privileges, if we are proud of these, it is just with God to blast them; even the temple, when it became Jerusalem's pride, was marred and laid in ashes. It is the honour of God to <hi type="italic">took upon every one that is proud and abase him.</hi>
entries.f08d89a814e8322a0b0a5fb82d15b0cb22384f4a: <div eID="gen17478" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Bottles Filled with Wine; Punishment Predicted; A Call to Repentance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  606.)</title> <div sID="gen17479" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore thou shalt speak unto them this word; Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, Every bottle shall be filled with wine: and they shall say unto thee, Do we not certainly know that every bottle shall be filled with wine? <hi type="super">13</hi> Then shalt thou say unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, even the kings that sit upon David's throne, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, with drunkenness. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy, but destroy them. <hi type="super">15</hi> Hear ye, and give ear; be not proud: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken. <hi type="super">16</hi> Give glory to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, before he cause darkness, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains, and, while ye look for light, he turn it into the shadow of death, <hi type="italic">and</hi> make <hi type="italic">it</hi> gross darkness. <hi type="super">17</hi> But if ye will not hear it, my soul shall weep in secret places for <hi type="italic">your</hi> pride; and mine eye shall weep sore, and run down with tears, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's flock is carried away captive. <hi type="super">18</hi> Say unto the king and to the queen, Humble yourselves, sit down: for your principalities shall come down, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the crown of your glory. <hi type="super">19</hi> The cities of the south shall be shut up, and none shall open <hi type="italic">them:</hi> Judah shall be carried away captive all of it, it shall be wholly carried away captive. <hi type="super">20</hi> Lift up your eyes, and behold them that come from the north: where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the flock <hi type="italic">that</hi> was given thee, thy beautiful flock? <hi type="super">21</hi> What wilt thou say when he shall punish thee? for thou hast taught them <hi type="italic">to be</hi> captains, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as chief over thee: shall not sorrows take thee, as a woman in travail? <div eID="gen17479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17480" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A judgment threatened against this people that would quite intoxicate them. This doom is pronounced against them in a figure, to make it the more taken notice of and the more affecting (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, every bottle shall be filled with wine;</hi> that is, those that by their sins have made themselves <hi type="italic">vessels of wrath fitted to destruction</hi> shall be filled with the wrath of God as a bottle is with wine; and, as every vessel of mercy prepared for glory shall be filled with mercy and glory, so they shall <hi type="italic">be full of the fury of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.20">Isa. li. 20</reference>); and they shall be brittle as bottles; and, like old bottles into which new wine is put, they shall burst and be broken to pieces, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.17">Matt. ix. 17</reference>. Or, They shall have their heads as full of wine as bottle are; for so it is explained, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">v. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">They shall be filled with drunkenness;</hi> compare <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Isa. li. 17</reference>. It is probable that this was a common proverb among them, applied in various ways; but they, not being aware of the prophet's meaning in it, ridiculed him for it: "<hi type="italic">Do we not certainly know</hi> that <hi type="italic">every bottle shall be filled with wine?</hi> What strange thing is there in that? Tell us something that we did not know before." Perhaps they were thus touchy with the prophet because they apprehended this to be a reflection upon them for their drunkenness, and probably it was in part so intended. They <hi type="italic">loved flagons of wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.3.1">Hos. iii. 1</reference>. Their watchmen were all <hi type="italic">for wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">Isa. lvi. 12</reference>. They loved their false prophets <hi type="italic">that prophesied to them of wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.11">Mic. ii. 11</reference>), that bade them be merry, for that they should never want their bottle to make them so. "Well," says the prophet, "you shall have your <hi type="italic">bottles full of wine,</hi> but not such wine as you desire." They suspected that he had some mystical meaning in it which prophesied no good concerning them, but evil; and he owns that so he had. What he meant was this, <div eID="gen17480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17481" type="x-p"/> 1. That they should be a giddy as men in drink. A drunken man is fitly compared to a bottle or cask full of wine; for, when the wine is in, the wit, and wisdom, and virtue, and all that is good for any thing, are out. Now God threatens (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.13">v. 13</reference>) that shall they shall all be <hi type="italic">filled with drunkenness;</hi> they shall be full of confusion in their counsels, shall falter in all their talk and stagger in all their motions; they shall not know what they say or do, much less what they should say or do. They shall be sick of all their enjoyments and throw them up as drunken men do, <reference osisRef="Job.20.15">Job xx. 15</reference>. They shall fall into a slumber, and be utterly unable to help themselves, and, like men that have drunk away their reason, shall lie at the mercy and expose themselves to the contempt of all about them. And this shall be the condition not of some among them (if any had been sober, they might have helped the rest), but <hi type="italic">even the kings that sit upon the throne of David,</hi> that should have been like their father David, who was <hi type="italic">wise as an angel of God,</hi> shall be thus intoxicated. Their priests and prophets too, their false prophets, that pretended to guide them, were as indulgent of their lusts, and therefore were justly as much deprived of their senses, as any other. Nay, <hi type="italic">all the inhabitants,</hi> both <hi type="italic">of the land</hi> and <hi type="italic">of Jerusalem</hi> were as far gone as they. Whom God will destroy he infatuates. <div eID="gen17481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17482" type="x-p"/> 2. That, being giddy, they should run upon one another. The cup of the wine of the Lord's fury shall throw them not only into a lethargy, so that they shall not be able to help themselves or one another, but into a perfect frenzy, so that they shall do mischief to themselves and one another (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will dash a man against his brother.</hi> Not only their drunken follies, but their drunken frays, shall help to ruin them. Drunken men are often quarrelsome, and upon that account they have <hi type="italic">woe and sorrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.29-Prov.23.30">Prov. xxiii. 29, 30</reference>); so their sin is their punishment; it was so here. God sent an evil spirit into families and neighbourhoods (as <reference osisRef="Judg.9.23">Judg. ix. 23</reference>), which made them jealous of, and spiteful towards, one another; so that <hi type="italic">the fathers and sons</hi> went <hi type="italic">together</hi> by the ears, and were ready to pull one another to pieces, which made them all an easy prey to the common enemy. This decree against them having gone forth, God says, <hi type="italic">I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy, but destroy them;</hi> for they <hi type="italic">will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy,</hi> but destroy one another; see <reference osisRef="Hab.2.15-Hab.2.16">Hab. ii. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen17482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17483" type="x-p"/> II. Here is good counsel given, which, if taken, would prevent this desolation. It is, in short, to <hi type="italic">humble themselves under the mighty hand of God.</hi> If they will <hi type="italic">hearken and give ear,</hi> this is that which God has to say to them, <hi type="italic">Be not proud,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.13.15">v. 15</reference>. This was one of the sins for which God had a controversy with them (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.9">v. 9</reference>); let them mortify and forsake this sin, and God will let fall his controversy. "<hi type="italic">Be not proud.;</hi> when God speaks to you by his prophets do not think yourselves too good to be taught; be not scornful, be not wilful, let not your hearts rise against the word, nor slight the messengers that bring it to you. When God is coming forth against you in his providence (and by them he speaks) be not secure when he threatens, be not impatient when he strikes, for pride is at the bottom of both." It is the great God that has spoken, whose authority is incontestable, whose power is irresistible; therefore bow to what he says, and <hi type="italic">be not proud,</hi> as you have been. They must not be proud, for, <div eID="gen17483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17484" type="x-p"/> 1. They must advance God, and study how to do him honour: "Give <hi type="italic">glory to the Lord your God,</hi> and not to your idols, not to other gods. Give him glory by confessing your sins, owning yourselves guilty before him, and accepting the punishment of your iniquity, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">v. 16</reference>. Give him glory by a sincere repentance and reformation." Then and not till then, we begin to live as we should, and to some good purpose, when we begin to <hi type="italic">give glory to the Lord our God,</hi> to make his honour our chief end and to seek it accordingly. "Do this quickly, while your space to repent is continued to you; <hi type="italic">before he cause darkness,</hi> before you will see no way of escaping." Note, Darkness will be the portion of those that will not repent to <hi type="italic">give glory to God.</hi> When those that by the fourth vial were scorched with heat <hi type="italic">repented not, to give glory to God,</hi> the next vial filled them with <hi type="italic">darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.16.9-Rev.16.10">Rev. xvi. 9, 10</reference>. The aggravation of the darkness here threatened is, (1.) That their attempts to escape shall hasten their ruin: <hi type="italic">Their feet shall stumble</hi> when they are making all the haste they can over <hi type="italic">the dark mountains,</hi> and they shall fall, and be unable to get up again. Note, Those that think to out-run the judgments of God will find their road impassable; let them make the best of their way, they can make nothing of it, the judgments that pursue them will overtake them; their way is dark and slippery, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.6">Ps. xxxv. 6</reference>. And therefore, before it comes to that extremity, it is our wisdom to give glory to him, and so make our peace with him, to fly to his mercy, and then there will be no occasion to fly from his justice. (2.) That their hopes of a better state of things will be disappointed: <hi type="italic">While you look for light,</hi> for comfort and relief, he will <hi type="italic">turn it into the shadow of death,</hi> which is very dismal and terrible, and make it <hi type="italic">gross darkness,</hi> like that of Egypt, when Pharaoh continued to harden his heart, which was darkness that might be felt. The expectation of impenitent sinners perishes when they die and think to have it satisfied. <div eID="gen17484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17485" type="x-p"/> 2. They must abase themselves, and take shame to themselves; the prerogative of the king and queen will not exempt them from this (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Say to the king and queen,</hi> that, great as they are, they must <hi type="italic">humble themselves</hi> by true repentance, and so give both glory to God and a good example to their subjects." Note, Those that are exalted above others in the world must humble themselves before God, who is higher than the highest, and to whom kings and queens are accountable. They must <hi type="italic">humble themselves,</hi> and <hi type="italic">sit down</hi>—sit down, and consider what is coming—sit down in the dust, and lament themselves. Let them humble themselves, for God will otherwise take an effectual course to humble them: "<hi type="italic">Your principalities shall come down,</hi> the honour and power on which you value yourselves and in which you confide, <hi type="italic">even the crown of your glory,</hi> your <hi type="italic">goodly or glorious crown:</hi> when you are led away captives, where will your principality and all the badges of it be then?" Blessed be God there is a crown of glory, which those shall inherit who do humble themselves, that shall never <hi type="italic">come down.</hi> <div eID="gen17485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17486" type="x-p"/> III. This counsel is enforced by some arguments if they continue proud and unhumbled. <div eID="gen17486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17487" type="x-p"/> 1. It will be the prophet's unspeakable grief (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If you will not hear it,</hi> will not submit to the word, but continue refractory, not only my eye, but <hi type="italic">my soul shall weep in secret places.</hi>" Note, The obstinacy of people, in refusing to hear the word of God, will be heart-breaking to the poor ministers, who know something of the terrors of the Lord and the worth of souls, and are so far from desiring that they tremble at the thoughts of the death of sinners. His grief for it was undissembled (his <hi type="italic">soul wept</hi>) and void of affectation, for he chose to weep <hi type="italic">in secret places,</hi> where no eye saw him but his who is all eye. He would mingle his tears not only with his public preaching, but with his private devotions. Nay, thoughts of their case would make him melancholy, and he would become a perfect recluse. It would grieve him, (1.) To see their sins unrepented of: "<hi type="italic">My soul shall weep for your pride,</hi> your haughtiness, and stubbornness, and vain confidence." Note, The sins of others should be matter of sorrow to us. We must mourn for that which we cannot mend, and mourn the more for it because we cannot mend it. (2.) To see their calamity past redress and remedy: "<hi type="italic">My eyes shall weep sorely,</hi> not so much because my relations, friends, and neighbours are in distress, but <hi type="italic">because the Lord's flock,</hi> his people and the sheep of his pasture, <hi type="italic">are carried away captive.</hi>" That should always grieve us most by which God's honour suffers and the interest of his kingdom is weakened. <div eID="gen17487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17488" type="x-p"/> 2. It will be their own inevitable ruin, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.19-Jer.13.21">v. 19-21</reference>. (1.) The land shall be laid waste: <hi type="italic">The cities of the south shall be shut up.</hi> The cities of Judah lay in the southern part of the land of Canaan; these shall be straitly besieged by the enemy, so that there shall be no going in or out, or they shall be deserted by the inhabitants, that there shall be none to go in and out. Some understand it of the cities of Egypt, which was south from Judah; the places there whence they expected succours shall fail them, and they shall find no access to them. (2.) The inhabitants shall be hurried away into a foreign country, there to live in slavery: <hi type="italic">Judah shall be carried away captive.</hi> Some were already carried off, which they hoped might serve to answer the prediction, and that the residue should still be left; but no: <hi type="italic">It shall be carried away all of it.</hi> God will make a full end with them: <hi type="italic">It shall be wholly carried away.</hi> So it was in the last captivity under Zedekiah, because they repented not. (3.) The enemy was now at hand that should do this (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lift up your eyes.</hi> I see upon their march, and you may if you will <hi type="italic">behold, those that come from the north,</hi> from the land of the Chaldeans; see how fast they advance, how fierce they appear." Upon this he addresses himself to the king, or rather (because the pronouns are feminine) to the city or state. [1.] "What will you do now with the people who are committed to your charge, and whom you ought to protect? <hi type="italic">Where is the flock that was given thee, thy beautiful flock?</hi> Whither canst thou take them now for shelter? How can they escape these ravening wolves?" Magistrates must look upon themselves as shepherds, and those that are under their charge as their flock, which they are entrusted with the care of and must give an account of; they must take delight in them as their beautiful flock, and consider what to do for their safety in times of public danger. Masters of families, who neglect their children and suffer them to perish for want of a good education, and ministers who neglect their people, should think they hear God putting this question to them: <hi type="italic">Where is the flock that was given thee</hi> to feed, <hi type="italic">that beauteous flock?</hi> It is starved; it is left exposed to the beasts of prey. What account wilt thou give of them when the chief shepherd shall appear? [2.] "What have you to object against the equity of God's proceedings? <hi type="italic">What will thou say when he shall visit upon thee</hi> the former days? <reference osisRef="Jer.13.21">v. 21</reference>. Thou canst say nothing, but that <hi type="italic">God is just in all that is brought upon thee.</hi>" Those that flatter themselves with hopes of impunity, what will they say? What confusion will cover their faces when they shall find themselves deceived and that God punishes them! [3.] "What thoughts will you now have of your own folly, in giving the Chaldeans such power over you, by seeking to them for assistance, and joining in league with them? Thus <hi type="italic">thou hast taught them against thyself to be captains</hi> and to <hi type="italic">become the head.</hi>" Hezekiah began when he showed his treasures to the ambassadors of the king of Babylon, tempting him thereby to come and plunder him. Those who, having a God to trust to, court foreign alliances and confide in them, do but make rods for themselves and teach their neighbours how to become their masters. [4.] "How will you bear the trouble that is at the door? <hi type="italic">Shall not sorrows take thee as a woman in travail?</hi> Sorrows which thou canst not escape nor put off, extremity of sorrows; and in these respects more grievous than those of a woman in travail that they were not expected before, and that there is no manchild to be born, the joy of which shall make them afterwards to be forgotten."
entries.c927a050f8081cd209de61d281bc200dabd3e056: <div eID="gen17488" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Punishment Predicted; Causes of Jerusalem's Ruin. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17489" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And if thou say in thine heart, Wherefore come these things upon me? For the greatness of thine iniquity are thy skirts discovered, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thy heels made bare. <hi type="super">23</hi> Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? <hi type="italic">then</hi> may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil. <hi type="super">24</hi> Therefore will I scatter them as the stubble that passeth away by the wind of the wilderness. <hi type="super">25</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy lot, the portion of thy measures from me, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; because thou hast forgotten me, and trusted in falsehood. <hi type="super">26</hi> Therefore will I discover thy skirts upon thy face, that thy shame may appear. <hi type="super">27</hi> I have seen thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy whoredom, <hi type="italic">and</hi> thine abominations on the hills in the fields. Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem! wilt thou not be made clean? when <hi type="italic">shall it</hi> once <hi type="italic">be?</hi> <div eID="gen17489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17490" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Ruin threatened as before, that the Jews shall go into captivity, and fall under all the miseries of beggary and bondage, shall be stripped of their clothes, <hi type="italic">their skirts discovered</hi> for want of upper garments to cover them, and their <hi type="italic">heels made bare</hi> for want of shoes, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.22">v. 22</reference>. Thus they used to deal with prisoners taken in war, when they drove them into captivity, <hi type="italic">naked and barefoot,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.20.4">Isa. xx. 4</reference>. Being thus carried off into a strange country, they shall be scattered there, <hi type="italic">as the stubble that is blown away by the wind of the wilderness,</hi> and nobody is concerned to bring it together again, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.24">v. 24</reference>. If the stubble escape the fire, it shall be carried away by the wind. If one judgment do not do the work, another shall, with those that by sin have made themselves as stubble. They shall be stripped of all their ornaments and exposed to shame, as harlots that are carted, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.26">v. 26</reference>. They made their pride appear, but God will <hi type="italic">make their shame appear;</hi> so that those who have doted on them shall be ashamed of them. <div eID="gen17490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17491" type="x-p"/> II. An enquiry made by the people into the cause of this ruin, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.22">v. 22</reference>. Thou wilt <hi type="italic">say in thy heart</hi> (and God knows how to give a proper answer to what men say in their hearts, though they do not speak it out; <hi type="italic">Jesus, knowing their thoughts,</hi> replied to <hi type="italic">them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.4">Matt. ix. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Wherefore came these things upon me?</hi> The question is supposed to come into the heart, 1. Of a sinner quarrelling with God and refusing to receive correction. They could not see that they had done any thing which might justly provoke God to be thus angry with them. They durst not speak it out; but in their hearts they thus charged God with unrighteousness, if he had <hi type="italic">laid upon them more than was meet.</hi> They seek for the cause of their calamities, when, if they had not been willfully blind, they might easily have seen it. Or, 2. Of a sinner returning to God. If there come but a penitent thought into the heart at any time (saying, <hi type="italic">What have I done?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">ch. viii. 6</reference>, wherefore am I in affliction? why doth God contend with me?) God takes notice of it, and is ready by his Spirit to impress the conviction, that, sin being discovered, it may be repented of. <div eID="gen17491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17492" type="x-p"/> III. An answer to this enquiry. God will be justified when he speaks and will oblige us to justify him, and therefore will set the sin of sinners in order before them. Do they ask, <hi type="italic">Wherefore come these things upon us?</hi> Let them know it is all owing to themselves. <div eID="gen17492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17493" type="x-p"/> 1. It is for the greatness of their iniquities, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.22">v. 22</reference>. God does not take advantage against them for small faults; no, the sins for which he now punishes them are of the first rate, very heinous in their own nature and highly aggravated—for <hi type="italic">the multitude of thy iniquity</hi> (so it may be read), sins of every kind and often repeated and relapsed into. Some think we are more in danger from the multitude of our smaller sins than from the heinousness of our greater sins; of both we may say, <hi type="italic">Who can understand his errors?</hi> <div eID="gen17493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17494" type="x-p"/> 2. It is for their obstinacy in sin, their being so long accustomed to it that there was little hope left of their being reclaimed from it (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Can the Ethiopian change his skin,</hi> that is by nature black, or the <hi type="italic">leopard his spots,</hi> that are even woven into the skin? Dirt contracted may be washed off, but we cannot alter the natural colour of a hair (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.36">Matt. v. 36</reference>), much less of the skin; and so impossible is it, morally impossible, to reclaim and reform these people. (1.) They had been long <hi type="italic">accustomed to do evil.</hi> They were taught to do evil; they had been educated and brought up in sin; they had served an apprenticeship to it, and had all their days made a trade of it. It was so much their constant practice that it had become a second nature to them. (2.) Their prophets therefore despaired of ever bring them to do good. This was what they aimed at; they persuaded them to cease to do evil and learn to do well, but could not prevail. They had so long been used to do evil that it was next to impossible for them to repent, and amend, and begin to do good. Note, Custom in sin is a very great hindrance to conversion from sin. The disease that is inveterate is generally thought incurable. Those that have been long accustomed to sin have shaken off the restraint of fear and shame; their consciences are seared; the habits of sin are confirmed; it pleads prescription; and it is just with God to give those up to their own hearts' lusts that have long refused to give themselves up to his grace. Sin is the blackness of the soul, the deformity of it; it is its spot, the discolouring of it; it is natural to us, we were shapen in it, so that we cannot get clear of it by any power of our own. But there is an almighty grace that is able to change the Ethiopian's skin, and that grace shall not be wanting to those who in a sense of their need of it seek it earnestly and improve it faithfully. <div eID="gen17494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17495" type="x-p"/> 3. It is for their treacherous departures from the God of truth and dependence on lying vanities (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">This is thy lot,</hi> to be scattered and driven away; this is <hi type="italic">the portion of thy measures from me,</hi> the punishment assigned thee as by line and measure; this shall be thy share of the miseries of this world; expect it, and think not to escape it: it is <hi type="italic">because thou hast forgotten me,</hi> the favours I have bestowed upon thee and the obligations thou art under to me; thou hast no sense, no remembrance, of these." Forgetfulness of God is at the bottom of all sin, as the remembrance of our Creator betimes is the happy and hopeful beginning of a holy life. "Having <hi type="italic">forgotten me, thou hast trusted in falsehood,</hi> in idols, in an arm of flesh in Egypt and Assyria, in the self-flatteries of a deceitful heart." Whatever those trust to that forsake God, they will find it a <hi type="italic">broken reed,</hi> a <hi type="italic">broken cistern.</hi> <div eID="gen17495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17496" type="x-p"/> 4. It is for their idolatry, their spiritual whoredom, that sin which is of all sins most provoking to the <hi type="italic">jealous God.</hi> They are exposed to a shameful calamity (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.26">v. 26</reference>) because they have been guilty of a shameful iniquity and yet are shameless in it (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.27">v. 27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have seen thy adulteries</hi> (thy inordinate fancy for strange gods, which thou hast been impatient for the gratification of, and hast even <hi type="italic">neighed</hi> after it), even the <hi type="italic">lewdness of thy whoredoms,</hi> thy impudence and insatiableness in them, thy eager worshipping of idols <hi type="italic">on the hills in the fields,</hi> upon the high places. This is that for which a <hi type="italic">woe</hi> is denounced against thee, <hi type="italic">O Jerusalem!</hi> nay, and many woes." <div eID="gen17496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17497" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is an affectionate expostulation with them, in the close, upon the whole matter. Though it was adjudged next to impossible for them to be brought to do good (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">v. 23</reference>), yet while there is life there is hope, and therefore still he reasons with them to bring them to repentance, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.27">v. 27</reference>. 1. He reasons with them concerning the thing itself: <hi type="italic">Wilt thou not be made clean?</hi> Note, It is the great concern of those who are polluted by sin to be made clean by repentance, and faith, and a universal reformation. The reason why sinners are not made clean is because they will not be made clean; and herein they act most unreasonably: "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou not be made clean?</hi> Surely thou will at length be persuaded to <hi type="italic">wash thee, and make thee clean,</hi> and so be wise for thyself." 2. Concerning the time of it: <hi type="italic">When shall it once be?</hi> Note, It is an instance of the wonderful grace of God that he desires the repentance and conversion of sinners, and thinks the time long till they are brought to relent; but it is an instance of the wonderful folly of sinners that they put that off from time to time which is of such absolute necessity that, if it be not done some time, they are certainly undone for ever. They do not say that they will never be cleansed, but not yet; they will defer it to a more convenient season, but cannot tell us when it shall once be.  <chapter eID="Jer.13"/> <div eID="gen17497" type="x-p"/>

entries.d249aa6acdcae032c6aa8c1af0bdc57a4c466aec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9882"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.27">Jr 13:1-27</reference>. Symbolical Prophecy (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.7">Jr 13:1-7</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen17537" type="x-p"/> Many of these figurative acts being either not possible, or not probable, or decorous, seem to have existed only in the mind of the prophet as part of his inward vision. [So Calvin]. The world he moved in was not the sensible, but the spiritual, world. Inward acts were, however, when it was possible and proper, materialized by outward performance, but not always, and necessarily so. The internal act made a naked statement more impressive and presented the subject when extending over long portions of space and time more concentrated. The interruption of Jeremiah's official duty by a journey of more than two hundred miles twice is not likely to have literally taken place.<div eID="gen17537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9882"/><hi type="bold">1. put it upon thy loins, &c.--</hi>expressing the close intimacy wherewith Jehovah had joined Israel and Judah to Him (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jr 13:11</reference>).<div eID="gen17538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">linen--</hi>implying it was the inner garment next the skin, not the outer one.<div eID="gen17539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put it not in water--</hi>signifying the moral filth of His people, like the literal filth of a garment worn constantly next the skin, without being washed (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.10">Jr 13:10</reference>). Grotius understands a garment not bleached, but left in its native roughness, just as Judah had no beauty, but was adopted by the sole grace of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.4-Ezek.16.6">Eze 16:4-6</reference>). "Neither wast thou washed in water," &c. <div eID="gen17540" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5ffa7aee60d59b4538151b55a12e9ddf2c1ceef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9883"/><div sID="gen17541" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9883"/><hi type="bold">4. Euphrates--</hi>In order to support the view that Jeremiah's act was outward, Henderson considers that the Hebrew Phrath here is Ephratha, the original name of Beth-lehem, six miles south of Jerusalem, a journey easy to be made by Jeremiah. The non-addition of the word "river," which usually precedes Phrath, when meaning Euphrates, favors this view. But I prefer English Version. The Euphrates is specified as being near Babylon, the Jews future place of exile.<div eID="gen17541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hole--</hi>typical of the prisons in which the Jews were to be confined.<div eID="gen17542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the rock--</hi>some well-known rock. A sterile region, such as was that to which the Jews were led away (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.7.19">Is 7:19</reference>) [Grotius]. <div eID="gen17543" type="x-p"/>
entries.684672a2aac3c3b59fe6ba0a23052353c33a5f76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9884"/><div sID="gen17544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9884"/><hi type="bold">6. after many days--</hi>Time enough was given for the girdle to become unfit for use. So, in course of time, the Jews became corrupted by the heathen idolatries around, so as to cease to be witnesses of Jehovah; they must, therefore, be cast away as a "marred" or spoiled girdle. <div eID="gen17544" type="x-p"/>

entries.a73bcc6c159eecf6b31a30fb2474a55406e98be0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9888"/><div sID="gen17549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9888"/>12. A new image.<div eID="gen17549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Do we not ... know ... wine--</hi>The "bottles" are those used in the East, made of skins; our word "hogshead," originally "oxhide," alludes to the same custom. As they were used to hold water, milk, and other liquids, what the prophet said (namely, that they should be all filled with wine) was not, as the Jews' taunting reply implied, a truism even literally. The figurative sense which is what Jeremiah chiefly meant, they affected not to understand. As wine intoxicates, so God's wrath and judgments shall reduce them to that state of helpless distraction that they shall rush on to their own ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">Jr 25:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.12">49:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Is 51:17</reference>, 21, 22; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.6">63:6</reference>). <div eID="gen17550" type="x-p"/>
entries.01232ab4a95489ca4c763d5e9f65daff8707b75e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9889"/><div sID="gen17551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9889"/><hi type="bold">13. upon David's throne--</hi>literally, who sit for David on his throne; implying the succession of the Davidic family (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.4">Jr 22:4</reference>).<div eID="gen17551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>indiscriminately of every rank. <div eID="gen17552" type="x-p"/>

entries.304d7222ef5356fde94939d5bb5f945e7b9aeaad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9891"/><div sID="gen17554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9891"/><hi type="bold">15. be not proud--</hi>Pride was the cause of their contumacy, as humility is the first step to obedience (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jr 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>). <div eID="gen17554" type="x-p"/>
entries.aad596a97b8faa01735cc8c7c9591d49d87c9c16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9892"/><div sID="gen17555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9892"/><hi type="bold">16. Give glory, &c.--</hi>Show by repentance and obedience to God, that you revere His majesty. So Joshua exhorted Achan to "give glory to God" by confessing his crime, thereby showing he revered the All-knowing God.<div eID="gen17555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stumble--</hi>image from travellers stumbling into a fatal abyss when overtaken by nightfall (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.30">Is 5:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.9">59:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">Am 8:9</reference>).<div eID="gen17556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dark mountains--</hi>literally, "mountains of twilight" or "gloom," which cast such a gloomy shadow that the traveller stumbles against an opposing rock before he sees it (<reference osisRef="John.11.10">Joh 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.35">12:35</reference>).<div eID="gen17557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow of death--</hi>the densest gloom; death shade (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.19">Psa 44:19</reference>). Light and darkness are images of prosperity and adversity. <div eID="gen17558" type="x-p"/>
entries.859552b3567ac9193a83825b7c5fd7d721916efd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9893"/><div sID="gen17559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9893"/><hi type="bold">17. hear it--</hi>my exhortation.<div eID="gen17559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in secret--</hi>as one mourning and humbling himself for their sin, not self-righteously condemning them (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.18">Php 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen17560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17561" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pride--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Jer.13.15">Jr 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.17">Job 33:17</reference>).<div eID="gen17561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flock--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.13.20">Jr 13:20</reference>), just as kings and leaders are called pastors. <div eID="gen17562" type="x-p"/>
entries.50c05f25a399173b7a9f2ce03140609cd2966714: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9894"/><div sID="gen17563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9894"/><hi type="bold">18. king--</hi>Jehoiachin or Jeconiah.<div eID="gen17563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">queen--</hi>the queen mother who, as the king was not more than eighteen years old, held the chief power. Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan, carried away captive with Jehoiachin by Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.8-2Kgs.24.15">2Ki 24:8-15</reference>).<div eID="gen17564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Humble yourselves--</hi>that is, Ye shall be humbled, or brought low (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.26">Jr 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.28.2">28:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your principalities--</hi>rather, "your head ornament." <div eID="gen17566" type="x-p"/>
entries.15a79e1c0d2372578e6f5bdffd6e99c0b7be3d6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9895"/><div sID="gen17567" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9895"/><hi type="bold">19. cities of the south--</hi>namely, south of Judea; farthest off from the enemy, who advanced from the north.<div eID="gen17567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shut up--</hi>that is, deserted (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.10">Is 24:10</reference>); so that none shall be left to open the gates to travellers and merchants again [Henderson]. Rather, shut up so closely by Nebuchadnezzar's forces, sent on before (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.10">2Ki 24:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.11">11</reference>), that none shall be allowed by the enemy to get out (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.13.20">Jr 13:20</reference>).<div eID="gen17568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wholly--</hi>literally, "fully"; completely. <div eID="gen17569" type="x-p"/>
entries.d43953085e95a1d7bab4e6136615ee8fbd87e0c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9896"/><div sID="gen17570" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9896"/><hi type="bold">20. from ... north--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar and his hostile army (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.14">Jr 1:14</reference>; 6:22).<div eID="gen17570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17571" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flock ... given thee--</hi>Jeremiah, amazed at the depopulation caused by Nebuchadnezzar's forces, addresses Jerusalem (a noun of multitude, which accounts for the blending of plural and singular, Your eyes ... thee ... thy flock), and asks where is the population (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jr 13:17</reference>, "flock") which God had given her? <div eID="gen17571" type="x-p"/>
entries.27ef8b19465cf4488cc464dd9c15988aac5faaea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9897"/><div sID="gen17572" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9897"/><hi type="bold">21. captains, and as chief--</hi>literally, "princes as to headship"; or "over thy head," namely, the Chaldeans. Rather, translate, "What wilt thou say when God will set them (the enemies, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.20">Jr 13:20</reference>) above thee, seeing that thou thyself hast accustomed them (to be) with thee as (thy) lovers in the highest place (literally, 'at thy head')? Thou canst not say God does thee wrong, seeing it was thou that gave occasion to His dealing so with thee, by so eagerly courting their intimacy." Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.2.18">Jr 2:18</reference>, 36; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>, as to the league of Judah with Babylon, which led Josiah to march against Pharaoh-necho, when the latter was about to attack Babylon [Maurer].<div eID="gen17572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sorrows--</hi>pains, throes. <div eID="gen17573" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a32d198aa7bcf99543f7097ad1ddc421074738c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9898"/><div sID="gen17574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9898"/><hi type="bold">22. if thou say--</hi>connecting this verse with "What wilt thou say" (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.21">Jr 13:21</reference>)?<div eID="gen17574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">skirts discovered--</hi>that is, are thrown up so as to expose the person (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.26">Jr 13:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.17">Is 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Na 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen17575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heels made bare--</hi>The sandal was fastened by a thong above the heel to the instep. The Hebrew, is, "are violently handled," or "torn off"; that is, thou art exposed to ignominy. Image from an adulteress. <div eID="gen17576" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0355c5ccb93d78e6d223273dea6d5090f5b4f3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9899"/><div sID="gen17577" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9899"/><hi type="bold">23. Ethiopian--</hi>the Cushite of Abyssinia. Habit is second nature; as therefore it is morally impossible that the Jews can alter their inveterate habits of sin, nothing remains but the infliction of the extremest punishment, their expatriation (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.24">Jr 13:24</reference>). <div eID="gen17577" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d0ab97521fc9230c25cee19ef00fcf0c77ece3b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9900"/><div sID="gen17578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9900"/>24. (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Psa 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen17578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the wind--</hi>before the wind.<div eID="gen17579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the wilderness--</hi>where the wind has full sweep, not being broken by any obstacle. <div eID="gen17580" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b37169604781a44059e497a3192369a131ce6f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9901"/><div sID="gen17581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9901"/><hi type="bold">25. portion of thy measures--</hi>the portion which I have measured out to thee (<reference osisRef="Job.20.29">Job 20:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>).<div eID="gen17581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">falsehood--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.13.27">Jr 13:27</reference>), false gods and alliances with foreign idolaters. <div eID="gen17582" type="x-p"/>
entries.c879cf9c29139331d0e924428ba780033ba6c974: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9902"/><div sID="gen17583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9902"/><hi type="bold">26. discover ... upon thy face--</hi>rather, "throw up thy skirts over thy face," or head; done by way of ignominy to captive women and to prostitutes (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Na 3:5</reference>). The Jews' punishment should answer to their crime. As their sin had been perpetrated in the most public places, so God would expose them to the contempt of other nations most openly (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.8">La 1:8</reference>). <div eID="gen17583" type="x-p"/>
entries.14debe36fd90dd8d470bfd0013ae673a27042646: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9903"/><div sID="gen17584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9903"/><hi type="bold">27. neighings--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.8">Jr 5:8</reference>), image from the lust of horses; the lust after idols degrades to the level of the brute.<div eID="gen17584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hills--</hi>where, as being nearer heaven, sacrifices were thought most acceptable to the gods.<div eID="gen17585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wilt thou not ... ? when--</hi>literally, "thou wilt not be made clean after how long a time yet." (So <reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">Jr 13:23</reference>). Jeremiah denies the moral possibility of one so long hardened in sin becoming soon cleansed. But see <reference osisRef="Jer.32.17">Jr 32:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.27">Lu 18:27</reference>. <chapter eID="Jer.13"/>

entries.f68294e688b8d2e60066760dcb1ce708198efd0d: <div eID="gen29595" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29596" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29597" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29597" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29596" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29598" type="x-p"/> This chapter contains an entire prophecy. The symbol of the linen girdle, left to rot for a considerable time, was a type of the manner in which the glory of the Jews should be marred during the course of their long captivity, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.11">Jer 13:1-11</reference>. The scene of hiding the girdle being laid near the Euphrates, intimated that the scene of the nation's distress should be Chaldea, which that river waters. The next three verses, by another emblem frequently used to represent the judgments of God, are designed to show that the calamities threatened should be extended to every rank and denomination, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.12-Jer.13.14">Jer 13:12-14</reference>. This leads the prophet to a most affectionate exhortation to repentance, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.15-Jer.13.17">Jer 13:15-17</reference>. But God, knowing that this happy consequence would not ensue, sends him with an awful message to the royal family particularly, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem in general, declaring the approaching judgments in plain terms, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.18-Jer.13.27">Jer 13:18-27</reference>. The ardent desire for the reformation of Jerusalem, with which the chapter concludes, beautifully displays the compassion and tender mercy of God. <div eID="gen29598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29599" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29600" type="x-p"/> Thus saith the Lord unto me - This discourse is supposed to have been delivered under the reign of Jeconiah, the son and successor of Jehoiakim, who came to the throne in the eighteenth year of his age; when the Chaldean generals had encamped near to Jerusalem, but did not besiege it in form till Nebuchadnezzar came up with the great body of the army. In these circumstances the prophet predicts the captivity; and, by a symbolical representation of a rotten girdle, shows the people their totally corrupt state; and by another of bottles filled with wine, shows the destruction and madness of their counsels, and the confusion that must ensue. <div eID="gen29600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29601" type="x-p"/> Go and get thee a linen girdle - This was either a vision, or God simply describes the thing in order that the prophet might use it in the way of illustration. <div eID="gen29601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29602" type="x-p"/> Put it not in water - After having worn it, let it not be washed, that it may more properly represent the uncleanness of the Israelites; for they were represented by the girdle; for "as the girdle cleaveth to the loins of a man, so have I caused to cleave unto me the whole house of Israel, and the whole house of Judah." And as a girdle is as well for ornament as use; God took them for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jer 13:11</reference>.
entries.a0318a3cde22cf41945ca37a5828b65ce09c4e4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29603" type="x-p"/> Go to Euphrates, and hide it there - Intending to point out, by this distant place, the country into which they were to be carried away captive.
entries.f397a03f16b36045890375eb2d0996593e105c63: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29604" type="x-p"/> And behold, the girdle was marred; it was profitable for nothing - This symbolically represented the state of the Jews: they were corrupt and abominable; and God, by sending them into captivity, "marred the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem," <reference osisRef="Jer.13.9">Jer 13:9</reference>.
entries.6136ede0a810ba4b6466fade19d6bb6c7a58be50: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen29604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29605" type="x-p"/> Every bottle shall be filled with wine? - The bottles were made for the purpose of being filled with wine; and it is likely, from the promising appearance of the season and the grapes, that there was a great likelihood of a copious vintage; and this made them say, "Do we not certainly know that every bottle shall be filled with wine? Have we not every prospect that it will be so? Do we need a revelation to inform us of this?"
entries.24cec7c28db717b0644186d52450ebaaa4369ad1: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29606" type="x-p"/> Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land - with drunkenness - You pretend to take this literally, but it is a symbol. You, and your kings, and priests, and prophets, are represented by these bottles. The wine is God's wrath against you, which shall first be shown by confounding your deliberations, filling you with foolish plans of defense, causing you from your divided counsels to fall out among yourselves, so that like so many drunken men you shall reel about and jostle each other; defend yourselves without plan, and fight without order, till ye all fall an easy prey into the hands of your enemies. The ancient adage is here fulfilled: - <div eID="gen29606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29607" type="x-p"/> Quos Deus vult perdere, prius dementat. "Those whom God determines to destroy, he first renders foolish."
entries.465dbfabe2bf1d596a76ff74f2d283f22161aba9: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29608" type="x-p"/> Give glory to - God - Confess your sins and turn to him, that these sore evils may be averted. <div eID="gen29608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29609" type="x-p"/> While ye look for light - While ye expect prosperity, he turned it into the shadow of death - sent you adversity of the most distressing and ruinous kind. <div eID="gen29609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29610" type="x-p"/> Stumble upon the dark mountains - Before you meet with those great obstacles, which, having no light - no proper understanding in the matter, ye shall be utterly unable to surmount.
entries.148cb59f251082af0ba60509775c09b4e80c38e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen29610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29611" type="x-p"/> My soul shalt weep in secret places - If you will not hearken to the Lord, there is no remedy: destruction must come; and there is nothing left for me, but to go in secret, and mourn and bewail your wretched lot.
entries.6c839a783af3d5abc55b925dab6be3865c8c3d27: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen29611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29612" type="x-p"/> Say unto the king and to the queen - Probably Jeconiah and his mother, under whose tutelage, being young when he began to reign, he was left, as is very likely. <div eID="gen29612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29613" type="x-p"/> Sit down - Show that ye have humbled yourselves; for your state will be destroyed, and your glorious crown taken from your heads.
entries.98df025128ade247018763f32f10cacbadf7ed0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen29613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29614" type="x-p"/> The cities of the south shall be shut up - Not only the cities of the north, the quarter at which the Chaldeans entered, but the cities of the south also; for he shall proceed from one extremity of the land to the other, spreading devastation every where, and carrying off the inhabitants.
entries.e6d41c6ad4425c2a134a23ff4952fd1c7470e845: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29615" type="x-p"/> Where is the flock - thy beautiful flock? - Jerusalem is addressed. Where are the prosperous multitudes of men, women, and children? Alas! are they not driven before the Babylonians, who have taken them captive?
entries.6045efe879515959de469bf84b86d46538a2cca2: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen29615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29616" type="x-p"/> Thou hast taught them to be captains, and as chief over thee - This is said of their enemies, whether Assyrians or Chaldeans: for ever since Ahaz submitted himself to the king of Assyria, the kings of Judah never regained their independence. Their enemies were thus taught to be their lords and masters.
entries.e391c8550a1067ef1a8eac7e86420579ae013da6: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen29616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29617" type="x-p"/> Are thy skirts discovered - Thy defenseless state is every where known; thou art not only weak, but ignominiously so. It is thy scandal to be in so depressed a condition; thou art lower than the basest of thy adversaries, and thou art so because of thy sin.
entries.dda3779515ec8793260be91c9135fd6acfa61a9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen29617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29618" type="x-p"/> Can the Ethiopian change his skin - Can a black, at his own pleasure, change the color of his skin? Can the leopard at will change the variety of his spots? These things are natural to them, and they cannot be altered; so sin, and especially your attachment to idolatry, is become a second nature; and we may as well expect the Ethiopian to change his skin, and the leopard his spots, as you to do good, who have been accustomed to do evil. It is a matter of the utmost difficulty to get a sinner, deeply rooted in vicious habits, brought to the knowledge of himself and God. But the expression does not imply that the thing is as impossible in a moral as it is in a natural sense: it only shows that it is extremely difficult, and not to be often expected; and a thousand matters of fact prove the truth of this. But still, what is impossible to man is possible to God. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jer.13.27">Jer 13:27</reference>.
entries.44b076f4eb9ab46a6556e48b39c781684efb44ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen29618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29619" type="x-p"/> The wind of the wilderness - Some strong tempestuous wind, proverbially severe, coming from the desert to the south of Judea.
entries.dae6e3ad44ae699e5052c381f4f12add2e6e71bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen29619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29620" type="x-p"/> Trusted in falsehood - In idols, and in lying prophets.
entries.afaf69409f80b25a28c240a0bc05fb007981a635: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen29620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29621" type="x-p"/> Therefore will I discover thy skirts upon thy face - It was the custom to punish lewd women by stripping them naked, and exposing them to public view; or by throwing their clothes over their heads, as here intimated. Was this the way to correct the evil?
entries.39b15d3504583efdb0139496e9ee18a59ba26ae8: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen29621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29622" type="x-p"/> I have seen thine adulteries - Thy idolatries of different kinds, practiced in various ways; no doubt often accompanied with gross debauchery. <div eID="gen29622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29623" type="x-p"/> Wo unto thee, O Jerusalem wilt thou not be made clean? - We see from this, that though the thing was difficult, yet it was not impossible, for these Ethiopians to change their skin, for these leopards to change their spots. It was only their obstinate refusal of the grace of God that rendered it impossible. Man cannot change himself; but he may pray to God to do it, and come to him through Christ, that he may do it. To enable him to pray and believe, the power is still at hand. If he will not use it, he must perish.  <chapter eID="Jer.13"/> <div eID="gen29623" type="x-p"/>

entries.e0b80083359c864ee33080b8ef8922c926f6cbc3: <reference osisRef="Jer.13.1-Jer.13.11">Jer 13:1-11</reference> <hi type="italic">The spoilt girdle. -</hi> Jer 13:1. <hi type="italic">"Thus spake Jahveh unto me: Go and buy thee a linen girdle, and put it upon thy loins, but into the water thou shalt not bring it.</hi> Jer 13:2. <hi type="italic">So I bought the girdle, according to the word of Jahveh, and put it upon my loins,</hi> Jer 13:3. <hi type="italic">Then came the word of Jahveh to me the second time, saying:</hi> Jer 13:4. <hi type="italic">Take the girdle which thou hast bought, which is upon thy loins, and arise, and go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in a cleft of the rock.</hi> Jer 13:5. <hi type="italic">So I went and hid it, as Jahveh had commanded me.</hi> Jer 13:6. <hi type="italic">And it came to pass after many days, that Jahveh said unto me: Arise, go to the Euphrates, and bring thence the girdle which I commanded thee to hide there.</hi> Jer 13:7. <hi type="italic">And I went to the Euphrates, and digged, and took the girdle from the place where I had hid it; and, behold, the girdle was marred, was good for nothing.</hi> Jer 13:8. <hi type="italic">And the word of Jahveh came to me, saying:</hi> Jer 13:9. <hi type="italic">Thus hath Jahveh said, After this manner will I mar the pride of Judah, and the great pride of Jerusalem.</hi> Jer 13:10. <hi type="italic">This evil people, which refuse to hear my words, which walk in the stubbornness of their heart, and walk after other gods, to serve them and to worship them, it shall be as this girdle which is good for nothing.</hi> Jer 13:11. <hi type="italic">For as the girdle cleaves to the loins of a man, so have I caused to cleave unto me the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, saith Jahveh; that it might be to me for a people and for a name, for a praise and for an ornament; but they hearkened not."</hi> <div eID="gen13981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13982" type="x-p"/> With regard to the symbolical action imposed on the prophet and performed by him, the question arises, whether the thing took place in outward reality, or was only an occurrence in the spirit, in the inward vision. The first view seems to be supported by the wording of the passage, namely, the twice repeated account of the prophet’s journey to the Phrat on the strength of a twice repeated divine command. But on the other hand, it has been found very improbable that "Jeremiah should twice have made a journey to the Euphrates, merely to prove that a linen girdle, if it lie long in the damp, becomes spoilt, a thing he could have done much nearer home, and which besides everybody knew without experiment" (Graf.). On this ground Ros., Graf, etc., hold the matter for a parable or an allegorical tale, But this view depends for support on the erroneous assumption that the specification of the Euphrates is of no kind of importance for the matter in hand; whereas the contrary may be gathered from the four times repeated mention of the place. Nor is anything proved against the real performance of God’s command by the remark, that the journey thither and back on both occasions is spoken of as if it were a mere matter of crossing a field. The Bible writers are wont to set forth such external matters in no very circumstantial way. And the great distance of the Euphrates - about 250 miles - gives us no sufficient reason for departing from the narrative as we have it before us, pointing as it does to a literal and real carrying out of God’s command, and to relegate the matter to the inward region of spiritual vision, or to take the narrative for an allegorical tale. - Still less reason is to be found in arbitrary interpretations of the name, such as, after Bochart’s example, have been attempted by Ven., Hitz., and Ew. The assertion that the Euphrates is called נהר פּרת everywhere else, including <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jer 46:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.6">Jer 46:6</reference>,<reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">Jer 46:10</reference>, loses its claim to conclusiveness from the fact that the prefaced rhn is omitted in <reference osisRef="Gen.2.14">Gen 2:14</reference>; Jer 51:63. And even Ew. observes, that "fifty years later a prophet understood the word of the Euphrates at Jer 51:63." Now even if <reference osisRef="Jer.51.63">Jer 51:63</reference> had been written by another prophet, and fifty years later (which is not the case, see on Jer 50ff.), the authority of this prophet would suffice to prove every other interpretation erroneous; even although the other attempts at interpretation had been more than the merest fancies. Ew. remarks, "It is most amazing that recent scholars (Hitz. with Ven. and Dahl.) could seriously come to adopt the conceit that פּרת is one and the same with אפּרת (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.7">Gen 48:7</reference>), and so with Bethlehem;" and what he says is doubly relevant to his own rendering. פּרת, he says, is either to be understood like Arab. <hi type="italic">frt</hi>, of fresh water in general, or like <hi type="italic">frdt</hi>, a place near the water, a crevice opening from the water into the land - interpretations so far fetched as to require no serious refutation. <div eID="gen13982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13983" type="x-p"/> More important than the question as to the formal nature of the emblematical action is that regarding its meaning; on which the views of commentators are as much divided. from the interpretation in <reference osisRef="Jer.13.9-Jer.13.11">Jer 13:9-11</reference> thus much is clear, that the girdle is the emblem of Israel, and that the prophet, in putting on and wearing this girdle, illustrates the relation of God to the folk of His covenant (Israel and Judah). The further significance of the emblem is suggested by the several moments of the action. The girdle does not merely belong to a man’s adornment, but is that part of his clothing which he must put on when about to undertake any laborious piece of work. The prophet is to buy and put on a linen girdle. פּשׁתּים, linen, was the material of the priests’ raiment, Eze 44:17., which in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.40">Exo 28:40</reference>; Exo 39:27. is called שׁשׁ, white byssus, or בּד, linen. The priest’s girdle was not, however, white, but woven parti-coloured, after the four colours of the curtains of the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="Exod.28.40">Exo 28:40</reference>; Exo 39:29. Wool (צמר) is in <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.18">Eze 44:18</reference> expressly excluded, because it causes the body to sweat. The linen girdle points, therefore, to the priestly character of Israel, called to be a holy people, a kingdom of priests (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>). "The purchased white girdle of linen, a man’s pride and adornment, is the people bought out of Egypt, yet in its innocence as it was when the Lord bound it to Himself with the bands of love" (Umbr.). The prohibition that follows, "into water thou shalt not bring it," is variously interpreted. Chr. B. Mich. says: <hi type="italic">forte ne madefiat et facilius dein computrescat</hi>; to the same effect Dahl., Ew., Umbr., Graf: to keep it safe from the hurtful effects of damp. A view which refutes itself; since washing does no kind of harm to the linen girdle, but rather makes it again as good as new. Thus to the point writes Näg., remarking justly at the same time, that the command not to bring the girdle into the water plainly implies that the prophet would have washed it when it had become soiled. This was not to be. The girdle was to remain dirty, and as such to be carried to the Euphrates, in order that, as Ros. and Maur. observed, it might symbolize <hi type="italic">sordes quas contraxerit populus in dies majores, mores populi magis magisque lapsi</hi>, and that the carrying of the soiled girdle to the Euphrates might set forth before the eyes of the people what awaited it, after it had long been borne by God covered with the filth of its sins. - The just appreciation of this prohibition leads us easily to the true meaning of the command in <reference osisRef="Jer.13.4">Jer 13:4</reference>, to bring the girdle that was on his loins to the Euphrates, and there to conceal it in a cleft in the rock, where it decays. But it is signifies, as Chr. B. Mich., following Jerome, observes, <hi type="italic">populi Judaici apud Chaldaeos citra Euphratem captivitas et exilium</hi>.
